extracted.intended_audience: Principal investigators and applicants seeking NIH grant funding (especially R01-equivalent applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for NIH grant applicants on how to plan submission volume, cadence, and target percentiles to maximize the probability of maintaining funding in a stochastic review system. Emphasizes realistic expectations and use of Institute/Center paylines and historical success rates to set goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission volume (vigor) — submit many proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the number of proposals you submit to raise your cumulative probability of at least one award; 'vigor is the thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric examples from the post: using a 17.7% success rate, 5 applications → 62.2% chance of ≥1 award, 10 → 85.7%, 15 → ≈95%. Using a 10.7% success rate (a more realistic target to hit a near-guaranteed funding verdict): ~9 proposals → ≈62%, ~18 → ≈86%, ~25 → ≈95%. The post emphasizes that probabilities do not add and that many submissions are required to reach high cumulative probabilities; be prepared for a lot of rejection and demoralizing experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target institute payline/percentile
rubrics_metrics.description: Set your target score based on your Institute/Center's apparent payline; aim to achieve a percentile that nearly guarantees funding rather than relying on luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: FY2023 apparent R01-equivalent payline at many ICs ~10–12%ile; the 50/50 transition is around 16–17%ile. The author personally targets an 8–9%ile score for their IC. Anything that funds above that is 'gravy.' Use RePORT and IC-specific data to determine realistic payline targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume stochastic/median outcomes (avoid special pleading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat funding as a probabilistic process; assume median outcomes rather than assuming you are inherently privileged or 'better than most.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against telling newcomers they are 'surely better than everyone else' and that they 'just need to write superior grants' — this advice sets people up for failure. Expect variance: some will do better, some worse, but plan based on expected (median) probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a steady submission cadence (at least one per deadline; consider ~3/year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit regularly — at minimum one application every deadline; some experienced commenters recommend ~3 submissions per year to sustain a career of mostly continuous funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter suggests that with roughly 10 submissions needed for ~95% chance (after accounting for triage), three submissions a year and four-year grant terms allows a career with continuous funding. The post endorses repeated trials as the best way to increase odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume institutional success rates apply to you
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about extrapolating a university's overall success rate to an individual PI's expected funding probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An institution may report a high success rate (>50% in some places), which affects the distribution of awards, but individual circumstances vary. The author warns it's a mistake for any PI to assume the institutional hit rate automatically applies to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand distribution of proposal quality and triage
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that reviewers categorize proposals roughly into terrible, salvageable, good, and outstanding — this shapes odds and what you need to submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer experience quoted: ~1/3 of proposals are 'terrible', ~1/3 'salvageable but have something wrong', ~1/4 'absolutely outstanding', ~1/12 'good but not great'. Many proposals are not so terrible that no reviewer could find value; disagreements among reviewers are common, especially in the middle tiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buy more 'tickets' — diversify reviewer samples via multiple submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because panels of three reviewers often disagree, the practical way to overcome reviewer subjectivity is to submit multiple proposals to get more independent samples of reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post uses the metaphor 'buy as many tickets (samples of three expert reviewers) as possible.' Multiple independent submissions increase the chance that at least one will be reviewed favorably by a particular sample of reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use IC-specific funding pattern data to set realistic goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult NIH RePORT and IC-level FY data (apparent paylines, success rates) to refine submission expectations and scoring targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author references the RePORT page on funding patterns by Institute/Center and FY2023 apparent paylines; recommends treating IC-specific apparent payline (~9–10%ile for the author's IC) as the operative target rather than NIH-wide averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept probabilistic outcomes; avoid personalizing failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the system yields variable individual outcomes; worse or better outcomes than predicted will occur for some PIs, and that is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post stresses that these are probabilities, not guarantees, and that 'you just don't get special pleading about how you are super unlucky' unless your actual hit rate substantially deviates from expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan submissions as part of a career funding strategy (realistic, persistent effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: View submission strategy as a long-game career plan: persistent, realistic submission effort can make an NIH-funded career attainable despite systemic flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post and commenters note the system is flawed and demoralizing, but argue that repeated submissions, realistic expectations, and strategic planning (target paylines, cadence, institutional context) can result in a career with mostly continuous funding; policy fixes (e.g., lotteries) would be structural improvements but are not a substitute for individual submission vigor.
